prompt: Write a short blog post about battling weeds. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# On the Conduct of a War Against Weeds

I have been at war with the weeds for some years now, and I am prepared to report that the weeds are winning. They do not say so; they are too well bred for that. They simply appear overnight in the bean row, looking as though they had been invited.

The first principle of the campaign is that a weed is merely a plant that has not been introduced to the right people. This is a comforting thought for about a minute. Then one notices that the purslane has taken over the path, and that the crabgrass has treaties with the neighboring lawn. At that point charity gives way to the hoe.

I am an advocate of the hoe. It is the one tool in the shed that allows a man to stand upright and think well of himself while he works. A sharp hoe, drawn through the soil on a dry morning, will do more damage to a weed than a whole afternoon of pulling; the sun finishes what the blade begins. A weed cut down in the morning and left on the surface is, by evening, a very sorry weed indeed. I find this satisfying in a way I would not care to explain to a stranger.

The second principle is timing. Weeds are creatures of habit, and they keep a calendar more exact than mine. The small ones are easy; they come away with a flick of the wrist and no argument. The large ones have roots, opinions, and a good deal of seed, and they must be dealt with in the manner of a treaty negotiation: slowly, firmly, and with a trowel. Let a dandelion go to seed, and you will spend the next three summers regretting a single afternoon's leniency.

The third principle is mulch. A thick layer of straw or shredded leaves over the bare ground will discourage most of the enemy before it has properly arrived. It is the garden equivalent of a closed gate; nothing is stopped entirely, but the visitors must at least put in some effort. My wife, who watches these operations from the porch with a patience I do not deserve, points out that I have been "about to mulch" since April. She is correct, and I have decided not to dispute the record.

I should add that I have tried the vinegar, the boiling water, and the newspaper. Each worked a little, and each made me feel clever for exactly one week. The weeds, I suspect, hold a meeting in the compost heap every Sunday to review my methods, and adjust.

Still, there is a quiet dignity in a clean row of onions, and I will not give it up. The war goes on; the hoe is sharp; the tea is hot. If the purslane wishes to negotiate, it knows where to find me.
